title: Basic Science Facts
description: Foundational science knowledge: solar system, human body basics, animal classification, states of matter, and Earth science essentials. Grade tagged from 2 through 6.
subject: science
source: Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) K-5 Earth/Space and Life Science performance expectations. Content reflects widely accepted elementary science curriculum.

items.prompt: What star is at the center of our solar system?
What planet do we live on?
What are the three states of matter we learn about first?
Which of these is an example of a LIQUID?
What do plants need to make food?
items.context: Plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide from the air to make their own food. This is called photosynthesis.

items.prompt: Which animal lays eggs?

items.context: Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, leaving 8 official planets.

items.prompt: Which planet is closest to the Sun?

items.context: Dolphins look like fish but they are mammals. They breathe air and feed milk to their young.

items.prompt: What are the planets in order from the Sun?

items.prompt: What is the main gas that makes up Earth's atmosphere?
items.context: Earth's atmosphere is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen. We think of oxygen as the important one because we breathe it, but nitrogen is by far the most common.

items.prompt: Which is NOT a vertebrate (animal with a backbone)?
items.context: Octopuses are invertebrates (mollusks). Fish, frogs, and snakes all have backbones.

items.answer: The continuous movement of water through evaporation, condensation, and precipitation

items.answer: Crust, mantle, outer core, inner core

items.prompt: What is the smallest unit of matter?
items.context: Atoms are made of smaller particles (protons, neutrons, electrons) but atoms are the smallest unit that retains the properties of an element.

items.prompt: What process do plants use to make their own food?
What is the boiling point of water at sea level in Fahrenheit?
items.context: Water boils at 212 F or 100 C at sea level. At higher elevations it boils at lower temperatures.
